assumptions: The API is a FastAPI/Starlette ASGI app; the limiter is implemented as ASGI middleware plus an optional per-route dependency/decorator for overrides. If the codebase is Flask/Django, the same design maps to a WSGI middleware + view decorator.

Redis is the storage backend so limits are shared across processes and replicas, with an in-memory backend used as a fallback for local dev and tests. The backend is chosen behind a small interface so it can be swapped.

Algorithm is a fixed-window counter implemented atomically in Redis (INCR + EXPIRE via Lua). Cheaper and simpler than sliding-window/token-bucket, at the cost of allowing up to 2x burst at a window boundary.

Identity for a limited caller is the authenticated principal (API key / user id from the existing auth context) when present, falling back to client IP derived from X-Forwarded-For (trusting the last N proxy hops, configurable) for anonymous traffic.
If Redis is unreachable, the limiter fails open (requests are allowed) and logs an error, so a cache outage cannot take the whole API down.

tasks.description: Add rate-limit configuration: a settings block (env-var driven, e.g. RATELIMIT_ENABLED, RATELIMIT_BACKEND, RATELIMIT_REDIS_URL, RATELIMIT_DEFAULT='100/minute', RATELIMIT_TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS) parsed into a typed config object, plus a parser for the 'N/period' limit string (second, minute, hour, day) that raises a clear error on malformed values. Include per-route override config as a mapping of route name/path -> limit string.

Define the storage backend interface (e.g. abstract `RateLimitBackend` with an async `incr(key, window_seconds) -> (count, ttl_remaining)` and `reset(key)`), and implement the in-memory backend with proper expiry and a lock for thread/task safety. This is the backend used in tests and local dev.

Implement the Redis backend against the same interface using a Lua script for an atomic INCR + EXPIRE-if-new, returning the current count and remaining TTL in one round trip. Wrap Redis calls so connection/timeout errors raise a dedicated `BackendUnavailable` exception rather than leaking redis-py errors.

Implement the core limiter: caller-identity resolution (authenticated principal first, then client IP from X-Forwarded-For honoring the configured trusted-hop count, then remote address), key construction (`ratelimit:{scope}:{identity}:{window_start}`), the fixed-window check that returns allow/deny plus limit, remaining, and reset timestamp, and fail-open behavior with an error log when the backend raises `BackendUnavailable`.

Add the middleware and wire it into the app: apply the default limit to all API endpoints, skip health/metrics/docs paths, and on rejection return HTTP 429 with the standard JSON error body and `Retry-After` plus `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, `X-RateLimit-Reset` headers. Set the same X-RateLimit-* headers on successful responses. Honor RATELIMIT_ENABLED as a global kill switch.

Add a per-route override mechanism (decorator/dependency such as `@rate_limit('10/minute')`) that the middleware consults via route metadata, so expensive or auth-sensitive endpoints can tighten or exempt (`@rate_limit(None)`) the default. Apply a stricter limit to the login/token endpoint as a first consumer.

Write tests: unit tests for the limit-string parser, both backends (counting, window rollover, expiry), and identity resolution including X-Forwarded-For spoofing with untrusted hops; integration tests hitting a real endpoint that assert the Nth request passes, N+1 returns 429 with correct headers, the counter resets after the window, limits are isolated per identity, per-route overrides win over the default, and a simulated Redis outage fails open.

Add operational glue and docs: structured log line on every 429 (identity, route, limit), a counter metric for allowed/throttled requests tagged by route, README/docs section covering configuration, the 429 contract and response headers for API consumers, and the fail-open behavior plus its security tradeoff.
